newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Deadline nears for Serbia's Milosevic, opposition.
newsitem.headline: Deadline nears for Serbia's Milosevic, opposition.

text.p: On the brink of an important political victory, Serbia's opposition is braced for any last-minute obstacles thrown up by the authoritarian President Slobodan Milosevic and his ruling Socialists.
Parliament meets on Tuesday to consider a bill reinstating victories by the Balkan country's three-party opposition coalition in local elections on November 17.

After months of daily protests by tens of thousands of people, as well as sharp criticism from Western powers, Milosevic announced last week he would ask parliament to recognise the disputed results of the municipal polls.
Ultra-nationalists of the Radical Party say they will challenge the constitutional basis of the bill.
"We shall certainly demand from the constitutional court an assessement...of the law," Radical leader Vojislav Seselj told the independent B-92 radio.
Milosevic's Socialists do not have a parliamentary majority in their own right but depend on the Radicals to carry through legislation.
This is not the only concern as the Tuesday deadline for the bill's passage into law approaches.

Law professor Vesna Rakic-Vodinelic, a legal adviser to the opposition Zajedno coalition, raised the issue of what the reinstatement of disputed or provisional municipal election results really meant.
In Serbia's second city, Nis, no provisional results were ever declared, she said. "It never even declared anything that could be called preliminary results," she said.

"In many municipalities these preliminary results do not cover all the seats in the local assembly. In Belgrade, for example, provisional results were declared for 100 seats out of the total of 110," she told the radio.
Rakic-Vodinelic also said the earliest the law could be put into effect would be 10 days after its passage through parliament with publication in the state gazette.
But it is the future of the long-term drive for political reform that worries the opposition as the daily marches and rallies visibly wind down ahead of Tuesday's parliamentary session.
Opposition politician Vuk Draskovic summed up the sense of unease and mistrust.

"We must never trust their (the Socialists') word, because those who stole our votes could easily have prepared a new manoeuvre," Draskovic told B-92. "Caution, caution, caution: we believe only in action, not words, parliaments or other institutions."
The opposition has also demanded free media and an independent judiciary ahead of parliamentary and presidential elections due by the end of this year.

Opposition coalition co-leader Zoran Djinjdic told a Budapest newspaper, Magyar Nezmet, that rallies would go on if news broadcast by state radio and television failed to be objective, the official Tanjug news agency reported.

"Milosevic was under extreme pressure for 80 days," said Vesna Pesic, leader of the only party in the opposition alliance committed to Western-style democracy. "It took him all of 80 days -- what then can we expect him to give us in the sphere of democratisation?"
